title: First coins struck in Lydia (Sardis)
summary: In Lydia, whose capital was Sardis, the earliest staters were struck in electrum, a natural gold-silver alloy, probably in the second half of the 7th century BCE. Around the middle of the 6th century BCE, King Croesus reformed the currency by issuing separate pure gold and silver coins.

uncertainty.note: Start is the second half of the 7th century BCE (-649 to -600) as dated by the first source; end is the middle of the 6th century BCE, the date given for the Croesus reform. Dating of the earliest issues is debated.

as_recorded.value: The earliest staters are believed to date to around the second half of the 7th century BCE.
around the middle of the sixth century

when.display: 2nd half of the 7th century BCE to c. 550 BCE

importance.justification: Lydian staters are cited as among the earliest coins, and the Croesus reform introduced separate gold and silver issues.

sources.title: The Importance of the Lydian Stater as the World's First Coin

reviewer_note: Least sure: the exact start. The sources hedge ("believed", "probably"), and the Sardis essay places the earliest electrum finds at Ephesus. The coin inscription read as Alyattes is only probable per that essay, so no ruler is named for the start.
